meaning: God's judgment on the enemy – the number 27,000 men fell at Aphek as a sign of the Lord's power over idolaters
description: The number 27000 appears in 1 Kings 20:30, where it is reported that 27000 Aramean soldiers died when the city wall of Aphek collapsed on them after their defeat by Israel. This event is part of a larger narrative in which Ben-Hadad of Aram challenged the God of Israel, and the Arameans claimed that the Lord was only a god of the hills and not of the plains (1 Kgs 20:28). God's response came as a crushing military defeat that demonstrated his sovereignty over all places and powers. The number 27000 thus represents the extent of God's judgment on a proud enemy and emphasizes that no one can defy the Lord without consequence. Although the number itself does not have a broad symbolic tradition in Jewish literature, it stands in the text as a testimony to God's absolute power and his willingness to defend his people when their enemies mock his name.

versions.meaning: The number 27,000 has no well-established or prominent symbolic meaning in biblical or Jewish tradition.
versions.description: 27000 is not a number that appears directly in the Bible with a clear symbolic role, nor does it have any known special meaning in classical Jewish numerology (gematria) or rabbinic literature. Mathematically, it is 30 × 30 × 30 (30 cubed), and the number 30 has certain biblical associations (such as the age when priests began their service), but the number 27000 itself is not assigned any recognized symbolic interpretation. Some may attempt to derive meaning through numerical combinations, but this would be speculative rather than grounded in traditional sources.

footnotes.text: Mathematically, 27,000 is 30 × 30 × 30 (30 cubed). The number 30 has several biblical associations, including the age at which priests and Levites began their service (Num 4:3), and the age when Joseph stood before Pharaoh (Gen 41:46). Whether this cubic structure holds any symbolic relevance for 27,000 in 1 Kings 20 is, however, speculative.

According to rabbinic tradition, Ben-Hadad's defeat at Aphek was seen as a consequence of the Arameans' blasphemous claim that Israel's God was limited to the mountains. Midrash literature emphasizes that God allowed judgment to fall precisely to demonstrate His universal sovereignty.
